newsitem.title: LEBANON: FEATURE - Lebanese man could be world's oldest at 135.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Lebanese man could be world's oldest at 135.

text.p: Jeanne Calment, move aside. According to official Lebanese records the oldest person in the world lives in Lebanon, not France, and he is a man, not a woman.

Former charcoal burner Ali Mohammed Hussein can hardly hear or see and his speech is unintelligible, but he still walks shakily around the remote, impoverished village of Qinieh in northeast Lebanon with the help of a walking stick.
The records say he is 135 years old.
His blue eyes are rheumy, his face is covered with a rough, white beard and his hands tremble as he sits hunched in a blanket on an old mattress in his one-room stone hovel.

Hussein's oldest surviving son Hammoudi, 62, shows his father's identity document. Issued in 1996, it says he was born in 1862 at Qinieh, a village of flat-roofed stone cottages in the rocky uplands of Akkar, Lebanon's northernmost province.
Hammoudi says previous IDs his father held were taken by journalists who promised to return them after photo-copying them.

The date on the card would make Hussein 13 years older than Calment, officially the oldest person in the world at 122, and 21 years older than Christian Mortensen of Denmark, who at 114 is believed to be the world's oldest man.
Hussein's age is also registered in Interior Ministry records at the nearby town of Koubayat.
Like all official records in Lebanon, his birth date is based on the country's only complete census, taken in 1932 under French rule.
BIRTH DATE BELIEVED CORRECT
Birth and death records were not kept systematically in Lebanon before 1932 and Hussein's remote northern village did not even appear in a partial census taken in 1921.
That means that information in the 1932 census may have come from word-of-mouth affidavits without documentary evidence to back it up.
However, a government official told Reuters he believed Hussein's 1862 birth date was correct.

Ghassan Shehadeh, director-general of the Interior Ministry's personal status department, tracked down the record of Hussein's birth at Reuters request in the ministry's microfilm copy of the 1932 census records.
"In the microfilm copy of our 1932 census records we found Ali Mohammad Hussein from Qinieh registered as born in 1862. We consider all information in this microfilm correct," Shehadeh said.
Hussein must have had an official identity card at the time, he added.
"Those who did not carry identity documents in 1932 were not registered or were registered as unknown nationality, so we consider Hussein's identity registration completely correct," Shehadeh said.
NOT GOOD ENOUGH FOR GUINNESS

But a spokeswoman in London for Guinness publishing, which issues the Guinness Book of World Records, said Hussein's lack of a birth certificate made it impossible to verify his age or challenge Calment's title of oldest person in the world.

"Without a birth certificate we would be unable to verify this report. Any other documents are not enough for our purposes," Guinness press officer Carol Jones told Reuters by telephone. Calment's title was based on her birth certificate, she said.
It is difficult to get details of his life out of Hussein himself.
Asked his age, he mumbles something about Turkish and French soldiers. Lebanon was in the Ottoman Empire until 1917 and was then under French mandate until 1943.
He wears the traditional black baggy pants of Lebanese mountain folk and an Arab headdress, a red and white chequered keffiyeh scarf held in place by braided black bands known as ikal.
Sometimes Hussein sings salacious songs for visitors in a low, croaking voice, encouraged by his wife, Amsha, who says she is 80 or 85 years old.
"Sing for them and they will give you money," Amsha said as a Reuters Television crew filmed him in his dirt-poor, smoke-blackened home.
"I wish I had time to give for the beautiful girls...," Hussein responds in a tuneless croak.
He looks in better physical shape than Jeanne Calment of France appears in photographs, but his family and neigbours are convinced he is very, very old.
COULD BE AS OLD AS 155, WIFE SAYS
"He has raised four or five generations. I am sure he is about 155 years old," said his wife.
Oum Khalid, a neighbour who says she is 80, said Hussein was already old when she was young. "Since I was young I remember Ali as old as he is now," she said.
According to his son Hammoudi, he has had 93 descendants including great-grandsons and great-granddaughters.
The secret of his longevity? Amsha says his diet is fresh milk and the green vegetables, leaves and herbs of the Lebanese countryside like silver beet, Swiss chard and wild thyme.
And he still smokes 60 cigarettes a day, says Amsha.
